story.logline: You feel well and roll up a sleeve; you may think the vaccine kills germs, but it trains your own cells, so what happens when the real germ arrives?

question: How does a vaccine teach my body to fight an infection?

source.title: How a vaccine teaches your body to fight an infection
source.publisher: Test fixture written for this repo
quotes: A vaccine trains your immune system to recognise a germ before you ever meet the real thing.
First, the vaccine shows the body a harmless piece or copy of the germ: a protein from its surface, a weakened version, or instructions that let your own cells make the protein for a short time.
Next, cells of the immune system find this unfamiliar protein and raise the alarm.
Specialist cells called B cells start making antibodies, which stick to the protein and mark it for destruction.
Other cells, called T cells, learn to find and destroy infected cells.
After the response settles down, some B and T cells stay on as memory cells, sometimes for years.
Finally, if the real germ arrives later, the memory cells recognise it at once.
The body makes antibodies within days instead of weeks, often before you feel ill.

Many people think a vaccine works like a medicine that kills the germ. It doesn't: it works by training your own immune system, which is why it has to be given before an infection, and why some vaccines need boosters as memory fades.
Vaccines can cause short-lived side effects such as a sore arm or a mild fever. These are signs of the immune system learning, not of the infection itself.

flows.label: A harmless piece of the germ

explain.caption: You feel well today. What does a vaccine do inside you?
The jab shows your body a harmless piece of a germ.
Your immune cells spot this stranger and raise the alarm.
B cells make tagging antibodies. T cells learn to kill infected cells.
A sore arm or mild fever is your body learning, not infection.
The response settles. Some cells stay on as memory, sometimes for years.
Later, the real germ arrives. Memory cells know it at once.
But the vaccine kills nothing. Your own trained cells stop the germ.
So the vaccine comes first, while you are still well.
Now weigh it up for yourself.

tradeoffs: A vaccine can cause a sore arm or mild fever for a short time, but these are signs of your body learning, not the infection.
A vaccine has to be given before an infection to help, so you have it while you still feel well.
Memory can fade, so some vaccines need boosters: longer protection can mean more visits.
leftOut: How well any one vaccine protects, and for how long; the article gives no numbers, so this picture has none.
How often side effects happen, and rare side effects; the article only names mild ones.
Differences between kinds of vaccine (a protein piece, a weakened germ, or instructions for your cells).
Your own health, age and any conditions that change how your immune system responds; check what applies to you.
questionsToAsk: Which kind of vaccine is this, and what does it show my body?
